evidence.claim: In 1943, the U.S. Army built the highway as an alternative connection from the Pacific to the Alaska Highway if the White Pass and Yukon Route railway was blocked.
evidence.quote: The highway was built by the U.S. Army in 1943 as an alternate route from the Pacific Ocean to the Alaska Highway, in case the White Pass and Yukon Route railway from Skagway should be blocked.

evidence.claim: After the war, blizzards and summer mudslides complicated travel, and maintenance was uneven.
evidence.quote: In the first decades after the war, maintenance was spotty at best; the road was plagued with blizzards in winter and mudslides in summer

evidence.claim: Year-round access followed in 1963.
evidence.quote: Year-round access was not achieved until 1963.

evidence.claim: Complaints over road conditions led to the congressionally funded Shakwak reconstruction project, begun in 1976, covering this highway and part of the Alaska Highway.
evidence.quote: Complaints over the condition of the road, primarily in Alaska, led to the U.S. Congress-funded Shakwak reconstruction project. This project, covering the Haines Highway and the portion of the Alaska Highway from Haines Junction to the U.S. border, began in 1976

evidence.claim: Klukwan is home to the Chilkat Indian Village, a federally recognized tribe headquartered here.
evidence.quote: The Chilkat Indian Village, a federally recognized tribe, is headquartered in Klukwan.

evidence.claim: The village stands on the north side of the Chilkat River, 21 miles northwest of Haines.
evidence.quote: It is 21 miles (34 km) northwest of Haines, on the north side of the Chilkat River near the Haines Highway.

evidence.claim: It began along the trading route later known as the Dalton Trail.
evidence.quote: Klukwan began as a Chilkat Tlingit village along the trade route later known as the Dalton Trail.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia gives its Tlingit name as Tlakw Áan, meaning roughly “forever village,” a reference to its antiquity.
evidence.quote: The name is Tlakw Áan in Tlingit, meaning roughly "forever village" due to its antiquity.

evidence.claim: The same account identifies Klukwan as the only remaining one of five Chilkat villages that existed in the area before 1900.
evidence.quote: Klukwan is the only remaining of five Chilkat villages that were in the area before 1900.

evidence.claim: Near the village, the glacier-fed Tsirku River ends in a delta four miles wide.
evidence.quote: The Tsirku River  is a glacier-fed stream in Southeast Alaska near the town of Haines in the U.S. state of Alaska.

evidence.claim: Near the village, the glacier-fed Tsirku River ends in a delta four miles wide.
evidence.quote: The river ends in a 4-mile (6 km) wide delta near the Tlingit village of Klukwan.

evidence.claim: Gold found along Porcupine Creek in 1898 brought a seasonal mining community into being.
evidence.quote: Gold was discovered along Porcupine Creek in 1898, and a seasonal community sprang up in the area.

evidence.claim: Porcupine lies across the Klehini River, about a mile southwest of highway Mile 35.
evidence.quote: It is located about 1 mile (1.6 km) southwest of Mile 35 of the Haines Highway, across the Klehini River.

evidence.claim: With a transient population, permanent buildings accumulated gradually.
evidence.quote: Due to the transient nature of the population, permanent structures were only gradually added to the area.

evidence.claim: When the district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1976, about 25 structures remained in varying states of decay.
evidence.quote: At the time the Porcupine District was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1976, about 25 structures were still standing in the area, in various stages of decay.

evidence.claim: Most dated from 1927 to 1936, when the Sunshine Mining Company was the largest operator in the area.
evidence.quote: Most of these were built during the period 1927–36, when the Sunshine Mining Company was the largest operator in the area.

flags: FHWA gives a 44-mile byway; Wikipedia gives 45 Alaska highway miles, while Haines-to-border figures vary. Kept the official byway scope distinct from the full highway.

Alaska DOT and FHWA place Klondike packhorse travel in the late 1880s; highway and Dalton Trail pages place relevant travel in the 1890s. Used the highway account’s 1898–1899 prospectors, omitting the conflicting official chronology.
Eagle totals and seasonal windows vary by source; used DOT’s hundreds and October–January for roadside roosting, without promising sightings.
Klukwan name spellings vary within the cache; used Tlakw Áan from the history paragraph. No tribal-authored cache page is available for its translation or five-village history.

Porcupine remains are documented only as of 1976; present condition and visitor access are unverified. Haines page dates the gold discovery to 1899; used the place-specific Porcupine page’s 1898 and flagged the conflict.
Material strip mileage runs toward Haines; reversed it to follow the Haines-to-border narrative.
Current Deishú translation omitted: Haines and Chilkoot Indian Association pages differ between end and beginning-and-end of the trail.
Porcupine moment remains short because the cache contains only a brief place history and no verified present access or condition.
